body: A plumber of about thirty is on his back under a kitchen sink in a house he has never been in before, with a torch in his mouth and somebody else’s cleaning things out on the floor beside him. The woman who owns the house has gone back upstairs. The radio on the windowsill is on, because it was on when he arrived and nobody has thought about it since. He has no idea what station it is. A song finishes and another starts, and somewhere in the second one he notices that he has been listening. At half eleven he packs up, and on the way out he says that whatever that was, it was all right.

Nobody chose that station for him and nobody explained it. He came into a stranger’s kitchen to do a job and heard whatever happened to be running, with no idea what it was or who it was meant for. That is not an edge case. That is the flagship’s actual job.

It is tempting to think of a flagship as the easy assignment — the broad one, the middle of the road, the station that never has to commit to anything. In practice it is the hardest brief on the band.

The word is naval and it repays being taken literally. A flagship is not the fastest ship, nor the newest, and frequently not the best armed. It is the one carrying the admiral and the signals, which means the rest of the fleet keeps station on it and reads it — and so does everybody on the horizon. Its job is legibility. A vessel that is hard to read is useless as a flagship however good it is at everything else, because the point is that the formation can look at it and know what is going on. The flagship of a radio band is the same object. It is the frequency people are handed when they arrive knowing nothing, and it may assume nothing whatever about who is reading it.

It sits at HM 308.70 on a dial of 121 stations, and it is the only frequency on the band carrying five bases rather than three — Sacramento, Denver, Houston, Miami and Honolulu, which is every time zone the United States keeps except Alaska.

That arrangement is a commitment, and so is the programming rule behind it, which is a rule about refusal. Nothing goes on the flagship that has to be explained before it can be heard, and nothing goes on it that would embarrass us in front of somebody who knows the subject. Those two filters remove a great deal of perfectly good material, including some of the best on the band. A specialist station only has to be right for its listener. The flagship has to be right for a stranger, and a stranger is the one audience nobody can ask.

Everything else has been moving the other way for twenty years. Segmentation is the whole business now — the feed tuned to a person, the playlist assembled for a mood, the promise, never stated and always kept, that nobody need encounter anything not made for them. It is comfortable, enormously effective, and it has quietly abolished the shared room. There is almost no surface left on which a believer of forty years and somebody who has never been inside a church might hear the same three minutes at once. Front doors have gone out of fashion, which is a strange thing for anybody in this business to have gone along with.

So the flagship runs continuous worship and teaching from the Inspire Family catalogue, day and night, and it will not play the same song twice in a day. The five bases exist so that a listener meets it on their own clock rather than somebody else’s morning. Nothing about the station is clever. Everything about it is arranged so that it can be walked in on halfway through, because halfway through is how almost everybody will meet it — a kitchen, a workshop, a waiting room, somebody else’s car.
The obvious objection is that broad means bland, and it is a good objection, because most of the time it does.

Be fair to it. Most middle-of-the-road stations are exactly what their critics say — the sound of a committee removing anything anybody might object to, until what is left is smooth, competent and unmemorable. Averaging is a real method with a real result, and the result offends nobody and reaches nobody either. But averaging is not the only way of being broad, and it is not the method here. Think of a hymn everybody in a full room can sing. It is not the average of their tastes; several of them would never have chosen it. It is the one thing that survived all of them, which is a different object entirely and much harder to find.
Broad is not the average of an audience. It is what survives all of them.

On a Sunday afternoon there are seven people in a kitchen and not enough chairs. The grandmother is eighty-one and has been in the same church since she was married in it. Her son-in-law has never been inside a church except for that wedding and two funerals, and finds the whole subject embarrassing on other people’s behalf. The radio is on above the fridge because somebody put it on when the potatoes went in. A song plays that the grandmother knows, and she gets some of the words of it quietly while looking for the serving spoon. The son-in-law, drying a dish beside her, notices nothing at all, because it is simply what is on. Nobody comments. Somebody asks whether there is any more gravy.

Two people who agree about nothing on this subject stood in the same room through the same three minutes, and neither was made uncomfortable and neither was patronised. That is not a small thing to build, and it is most of the brief.

Here is what it costs, and the cost is real. The flagship will almost never be anybody’s favourite station. A specialist frequency gets loved; people belong to it and defend it. The flagship gets used. Anybody who genuinely loves country gospel will have found Gospel Country inside a fortnight and be happier there, and anybody who wants the long contemplative night will end up at Midnight Praise and stay. Both are the system working as designed, and both are listeners the flagship has handed away.

But nobody decorates a hallway, and everybody comes through it. Being the second-favourite station of a great many people is not a consolation prize; it is the function, and it is the one role on the dial that cannot be filled by anybody with a strong opinion. The flagship exists so that the specialists are free to be specialist. Every frequency further down the band can assume something about its listener precisely because there is one number where nothing is assumed at all.

So the rule stands as written. Nothing goes on the flagship that needs explaining first, and nothing goes on it that would embarrass us in front of somebody who knows the subject. What survives both filters is not the average of the band and not the safest material on it. It is the part of this catalogue that can be walked in on by a stranger and still be true enough for somebody who has been singing it for forty years — and that, rather than anything about reach or scale, is what makes a station the flagship.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. Every one of them assumes something about who is listening. One of them does not.

So start where the strangers start: HM 308.70 — Year of Jubilee. It is the front door of the band, running continuous worship and teaching from the Inspire Family catalogue day and night, on five bases across five time zones so it meets you at your own hour. It is the station to leave on when the house is full of people who do not all believe the same things, or when you cannot face a decision about music at all. Everything on it has been through the two filters — it needs no explaining, and it would not embarrass us in front of somebody who knows the subject. That is a narrow gate for a song, and what comes through it is the station.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer, on the article’s own terms. Do not put HM 308.70 on to evaluate it. Put it on this week at an hour when somebody is coming to the house who shares none of this — the plumber, the neighbour, your daughter’s new boyfriend — then get on with what you were doing and do not mention it. If it has been built properly, nobody will remark on it at all, and one of them will notice, somewhere in the second song, that they have been listening.
